subject: Anatomy
summary: The pubis is the anterior inferior portion of the pelvic bone, forming the lower front of the bony pelvis and contributing to the acetabulum and pubic symphysis. It serves as attachment for muscles and ligaments that support the lower abdomen and thigh.

sections.p: The pubis is a paired bone that joins at the midline to form the pubic symphysis, a fibrocartilaginous joint. It is a key landmark for many clinical examinations.
b: Forms the anterior wall of the pelvis
Contributes to the acetabulum
Site of attachment for adductor and abdominal muscles

sections.p: Each pubic bone has a body, superior and inferior rami, and a pubic crest. The superior ramus joins the ilium at the acetabulum; the inferior ramus joins the ischium.
b: Body: central thick portion
Superior ramus: long, thin, forms part of acetabulum
Inferior ramus: short, joins ischium

sections.p: Anteriorly lies the skin and subcutaneous tissue; posteriorly the bladder and urethra. Laterally the obturator nerve and vessels pass near the inferior ramus.
b: Bladder lies directly posterior
Obturator neurovascular bundle runs along inferior ramus
Femoral vessels pass just inferior to the pubic tubercle

sections.p: Supplied by branches of the external iliac artery (inferior epigastric) and the obturator artery.
b: Inferior epigastric artery supplies the superior ramus
Obturator artery supplies the inferior ramus

sections.p: Sensory innervation comes from the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, and genitofemoral nerves.
b: Iliohypogastric: skin over pubic region
Ilioinguinal: skin of upper medial thigh
Genitofemoral: scrotum/labia majora

sections.p: Provides attachment for the adductor longus, gracilis, and rectus abdominis, helping with thigh adduction and trunk flexion. The symphysis allows limited movement for childbirth.
b: Muscle attachment for thigh adductors
Supports lower abdominal wall
Allows slight movement during parturition

sections.p: Pubic injuries can present as fractures, osteitis pubis, or symphysis diastasis. In low‑resource settings, osteomyelitis from TB or chronic infection is common.
b: Pubic fracture: pain on weight‑bearing, palpable step-off
Osteitis pubis: chronic groin pain, often post‑sports
Symphysis diastasis: widening >2 cm in pregnancy
TB osteomyelitis: night pain, systemic symptoms

t.b: Does it show fracture or diastasis? A visible break or >2 cm separation confirms diagnosis.
Is there bone marrow edema or abscess? Positive findings support osteitis or infection.
Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? Positive result guides anti‑TB therapy.

sections.p: Palpate the pubic symphysis for tenderness, assess for step‑off, and compare bilateral femoral pulses. In pregnancy, measure symphysis width with ultrasound if diastasis suspected.
b: Tenderness over symphysis suggests osteitis or fracture
Asymmetry of femoral pulses may indicate vascular injury
Symphysis width >2 cm in late pregnancy warrants obstetric review

whenToSeekHelp: Severe groin pain with inability to bear weight
Fever, night sweats, and worsening pelvic pain (possible infection)
Rapidly expanding swelling or signs of sepsis

faq.a: A fibrocartilaginous joint where the two pubic bones meet at the midline.

faq.q: Why does the pubic bone matter in childbirth?
faq.a: It allows slight widening of the pelvic outlet, facilitating fetal passage.

faq.q: How can you differentiate a pubic fracture from osteitis pubis?
faq.a: Fracture shows a clear break on X‑ray; osteitis shows diffuse pain and MRI bone edema without a line.

exam: Describe the bony landmarks of the pubis and their clinical significance.
Explain how to assess for symphysis pubis diastasis in a pregnant patient.
List the common causes of pubic pain in low‑resource settings and the initial investigations.
